subject: industrial-systems
audience: FE Industrial & Systems candidates and industrial engineering students
title: The Assembly Line That Needed 4 Stations, Not 3.6
featured_title: THE ASSEMBLY LINE THAT NEEDED 4 STATIONS, NOT 3.6

presentation.challenge: The arithmetic produced 3.6 stations, but a production line cannot operate with a fraction of a station. The theoretical minimum was 4.

practice.topic: Manufacturing, Service, and Other Production Systems
practice.primary_question: How are required cycle time and the theoretical minimum number of workstations calculated for an assembly line?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Computing total task time divided by cycle time and reporting the noninteger result directly instead of rounding up to a feasible whole number of stations.

breadcrumb.name: Manufacturing, Service, and Other Production Systems

case_dna.target_misconception: If total task time divided by cycle time equals 3.6, the line requires 3.6 workstations.
case_dna.why_plausible: The ratio is mathematically correct as a lower-bound workload measure, but physical workstations are discrete resources.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With 450 productive minutes per shift and demand of 225 units, cycle time is 2.0 min/unit. Total task time is 7.2 min, so 7.2/2.0=3.6 and the theoretical minimum feasible station count is ceil(3.6)=4.
case_dna.corrected_model: Calculate cycle time as available production time divided by required output, divide total task time by cycle time, then round up to the next whole workstation.

problem_statement: An assembly line has 450 productive minutes available per shift and must produce 225 units per shift. The sum of all elemental task times is 7.2 minutes per unit. A planning note calculates 7.2/2.0=3.6 and reports that 3.6 stations are required. Determine the required cycle time, the theoretical minimum number of stations, and the line efficiency if four stations are used.
fixed_constraints: Assume a feasible precedence assignment exists with four stations

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The workload ratio was correct. The resource count was not.
gates.prompt: What must be calculated before determining the station count?

options.label: Use C=available time/output, then Nmin=ceil(total task time/C)
options.reason: Cycle time sets the workload capacity of each station, and a station count must be a whole number.

options.label: Use N=total task time/C and keep the decimal result
options.reason: A fractional workstation is not a feasible physical resource count.

options.label: Round 3.6 down to 3 stations
options.reason: Three stations provide only 6.0 min of work capacity per cycle, less than the required 7.2 min.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the theoretical minimum number of stations
gates.prompt: Enter the minimum whole number of stations.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Test the production capacity
gates.running_label: BALANCING WORK CONTENT AGAINST CYCLE TIME…

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the workstation requirement
gates.prompt: Calculate C=450/225 and Nmin=ceil(7.2/C). Enter the station count.
gates.hint: Round the workload ratio up, not to the nearest integer.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Three stations cannot carry the required work content

cards.text: Four stations provide 8.0 min of station-time capacity per cycle; three provide only 6.0 min.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the line-design note
report: C1. Required cycle time is 2.0 min/unit.
C2. Total task time is 7.2 min/unit.
C3. Therefore the line needs 3.6 workstations.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: This is the stated total work content.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: A physical line cannot use 0.6 of a workstation, and rounding down would violate the cycle-time capacity requirement.

evidence_choices.label: ceil(7.2/2.0)=4
evidence_choices.reason: The theoretical minimum feasible count is the ceiling of the workload ratio.

correction.template: The required cycle time is {cycle_time} min/unit and the theoretical minimum is {stations} stations.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Evaluate the four-station line
gates.constraint: Use four stations and the 2.0 min cycle time.

options.label: Line efficiency is 100%
options.reason: The four stations provide 8.0 min of capacity per cycle, leaving 0.8 min of balance delay.

options.label: Line efficiency is 72%
options.reason: That does not use the station count and cycle time correctly.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Recalculate for lower required output
gates.prompt: If the same line has 450 productive minutes and demand falls to 180 units/shift, what is the theoretical minimum number of stations?

options.label: 2 stations
options.reason: Two stations provide only 5.0 min of capacity per cycle.

options.label: 4 stations
options.reason: Four may be used, but the theoretical minimum becomes three.

gates.explanation: Lower required output increases allowable cycle time and can reduce the minimum workstation count.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the assembly-line calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that workstation requirements are discrete and that the theoretical minimum station count is rounded up from total work content divided by cycle time.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A fractional workload ratio was reported as a feasible workstation count.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Workstations are discrete resources and must provide enough capacity within each cycle.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use C=available time/demand and Nmin=ceil(total task time/C).

seo.seo_title: Assembly Line Cycle Time and Minimum Stations | FE E-081
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Industrial & Systems Case E-081: 450 min for 225 units gives a 2.0 min cycle time, so 7.2 min of work needs at least 4 stations.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Industrial assembly line cycle time minimum stations
seo.excerpt: A line-balancing calculation can produce a fractional workload ratio, but the physical workstation count must be rounded up.
seo.direct_answer: Cycle time is 450/225=2.0 min/unit. The workload ratio is 7.2/2.0=3.6, so the theoretical minimum is 4 stations. With four stations, line efficiency is 7.2/(4×2.0)=90%.

faqs.q: How do you calculate assembly-line cycle time?
faqs.a: Divide available production time by required output.

faqs.q: Why is 3.6 workstations rounded up to 4?
faqs.a: Because workstation count is discrete and three stations would not provide enough work capacity per cycle.
